summary: Sell the S&P 500 fund: it ended Wednesday below its 200-day average, the line I set for selling it, so I keep that promise even though futures point higher this morning; the equal-weight fund and the health care fund stay, and the cash waits for a clear buy-back signal or 10 December at the latest.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Wednesday 18 November it was worth $972.52 against $961.03 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. Both are down; the account has lost less because a quarter of it is in cash and the rest leans away from the giant technology companies. Six trading days is too short to call that lead skill.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Wednesday was a fifth straight down day for the S&P 500, its longest losing streak since June. The S&P 500 fund SPY fell 0.31% and the Dow fund DIA 1.10%, while the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ rose 0.39%. Nvidia rose before the open on its strong results, then reversed and ended down about 2.9%.
- The notes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting said almost all officials expect further rate increases to be appropriate, and a couple said an increase larger than a quarter point could be considered in December if inflation figures disappoint. Fed Governor Waller said a half-point increase is probably needed on 9 December. Officials also discussed the risk that spending on AI may not pay off.
- Health care insurers fell hard for a second day: UnitedHealth about 10%, Humana about 13%, Elevance about 8%. The cause is a proposal from Medicare's administrator, published on Monday, to use audit results more widely to recover overpayments to Medicare Advantage insurers, which it estimates at $90.2 billion from 2027 to 2036. Comments are open until 19 January 2027. The health care fund XLV fell 2.2%.
- Oil fell again; US crude ended near $82 after a rise in US stockpiles, and energy was the weakest sector.
- This morning, before the open, futures pointed to the S&P 500 about 1% higher and the Nasdaq 100 about 2% higher, the day the year's largest new share listing (Anthropic, priced at $83 a share) begins trading. The 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.07%. Weekly jobless claims and the Philadelphia Fed factory survey come out at 8:30 a.m. New York time, after this was written. A newly listed share cannot be bought here until it has 20 sessions of trading history, and I would not chase it on day one in any case.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. SPY: sell all of it. When I bought it I wrote that it would be cut if it ended a day below its 200-day average, and on 18 November I wrote that the next decision would sell it if that happened. It ended Wednesday at $730.20, below its 200-day average of $732.55. The line was broken, so I sell. I thought hard about this morning's futures, which point to an open about 1% higher, likely back above the line. Waiting for that bounce would mean moving the line after the fact, which is exactly what the rule is there to prevent, and the evidence behind it has not improved: five down days, a Fed that is preparing to raise rates by possibly half a point, a 10-year yield above 5%, and SPY 4% below its 50-day average. If the market does recover, the cost of being wrong is one round of fees on about $290, roughly $1, plus whatever rise is missed before the buy-back signal.

2. RSP: keep. It ended at $215.43, 0.2% above its 50-day average ($214.98), the level that sends it back out. The reason for owning it is still working: over 20 trading days it is down 0.6% while SPY is down 5.6%. It is very close to its line. If it ends a day below its 50-day average, the next decision sells it, and with SPY already sold the proceeds would stay in cash rather than move into SPY.

3. XLV: keep, with the reason for doubt written down. When I bought it I wrote that a concrete change in US insurance policy that undercuts the sector would prove it wrong. The Medicare Advantage audit proposal is a real policy change aimed at part of the sector, so I checked it against that test. It hits the health insurers, which are roughly a tenth of the fund; drug makers, device makers and hospitals make up most of the rest. It is a proposal with a comment period to January, not a final rule. The price lines still hold: XLV ended at $181.17, about 3% above its 50-day average ($176.03) and about 5% below what I paid, short of the 8% loss limit (about $175). I would not buy more today, but the case for holding has weakened rather than broken. If it ends a day below $176, or if the rule is widened to cut payments for drug makers or hospitals, the next decision sells it.

4. Cash. After the sale the account will hold about $540 in cash, about 55%. That is a large bet against a benchmark that is fully invested, so it needs a reason and an end date. The reason: the broad market has broken its long-run trend just as the Fed is preparing to raise rates, possibly by half a point. The end date stays as written on 12 November: fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December. The new buy-back signal comes first if it arrives: SPY ending two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average (about $740 today). I looked again at a Treasury bill fund (SGOV) for the cash; for a stay of three weeks or less, the interest is about the same as the fees, so it stays as plain cash. Gold (GLD) is in a steep fall, down 20% in 60 days, and is not a shelter right now.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: The biggest risk is selling right before a rebound: futures point to a 1% higher open, and if the market recovers quickly the account, with about 55% in cash, will fall behind a fully invested benchmark, and buying SPY back later will cost a second round of fees at a higher price. RSP is only 0.2% above its own line and may have to be sold soon too, leaving the account mostly in cash. Health care could keep falling if the Medicare proposal is made broader or if investors stop treating the sector as shelter. A half-point Fed increase on 9 December could push long-term rates higher and hurt everything the account holds. Futures and before-the-open prices can change by 9:30, and the jobless claims figures were not out when this was written.
strategy_change: Version 2 of the plan adds a section on selling and buying back. A broken line means a sale and the line is not moved after the fact. After SPY is sold for ending below its 200-day average, it is bought back once it ends two trading days in a row at least 1% above that average, so the account does not pay fees to step in and out while the price hovers at the line. Cash above a quarter of the account must carry a written date by which it goes back into the market.

orders.reason: Ended 18 November at $730.20, below its 200-day average of $732.55, the line set for selling it when it was bought.
